Story
What many of you don't know is that I once auditioned for the Churchill Show.
Around 2014, after dropping out of campus, I resorted to writing and sharing short jokes on my old Facebook account to cope with the pangs of dropping out. I was actually good at it.
Then one day, one of my jokes went viral and caught the attention of Mwalimu Churchill himself. He commented on my wall and invited me to audition at JKUAT during one of his Churchill Live Campus Tour editions.
Man, I was excited. I started envisioning myself sharing stages with kina Chipukeezy, kina Eric Omondi and kina YY, cracking ribs on national television and eventually becoming a household name.
The problem was that I spent more time dreaming about being famous than rehearsing my jokes. I walked on the stage and immediately tensed. There is nothing as scary as standing on stage, with hundreds of hungry Juja boys staring at you, half of them high on weed, and the other half starving.
I forgot half my jokes on stage, and the half I remembered, I butchered.  They booed me off. They booed me so hard I almost thought I was the one responsible for disbursing their HELB loans, or giving them upkeep money.
I was temporarily staying at Versity House, my cousin's hostel. Walking back to the hostels, my cousin looked at me and said: "You are very funny, bro. I laughed hard."
"Then why was I booed if I'm funny?"
He looked me dead in the eye. "Kenyans don't have the brains to consume your jokes. Your jokes are in the range of Dave Chappelle, Chris Rock, and Kevin Hart. They wanted jokes about Luhyas being foodious, Kikuyus loving money, Kambas snitching, and Luos being extravagant. You are too smart for them."
Somehow, this calmed me down.  I chose to believe him, but I knew he was lying to me.  I decided to try again. Not long after, I saw a poster inviting university students to a talent show at the University of Nairobi cafeteria.
I convinced myself that I could crack it here. This time, I wrote properly. I rehearsed properly. I prepared myself mentally. Then, I got on stage, and again,  no one laughed. Again, I was booed heavily. I should have walked off. Instead, I stood there and let it happen, hoping the crowd would eventually change its mind.
Then, right as the booing was dying down, one female comrade took advantage of the silence and shouted: "Before coming here, did you stand before your mirror and crack those jokes to yourself? Were they funny? Did they make you laugh?"
The whole cafeteria erupted into laughter. Man, I wished the stage opened wide and swallowed me at that time. I should have left it there. I should have walked off stage at that time. But because humiliation apparently had not yet finished with me, I waited for the laughter to die down and replied: "I don't have a mirror at home."
She didn't even blink. Immediately, she responded, "No wonder you left your house with uncombed hair and a shirt with a torn collar."
The place went up again, louder this time. Someone else shouted: "The girl should be on stage, not him! She is funnier" At that point, I wanted the ground to open and swallow me.
I remember the MC running towards the stage to rescue me. I was too weak to walk or respond. When the MC picked up the microphone and whispered something in my ear, another comrade shouted, "Have you tried cracking these jokes to students of Kabianga University?"
I don't remember how I got off that stage. What I remember is walking away from UoN and deciding that stand-up comedy was not my thing. Maybe I was only built to deliver jokes in written form.
As I do now.
